s92-perf-001.text: What performance credit may be taken for engines delivering above-specification power (a positive power margin)? -- Correct: No performance credit is to be taken for above specification power. The performance charts are predicated on engines that deliver specification power; no performance credit is to be taken for above-specification power (positive power margin).
s92-perf-001.note: p.4-1 (DOC 213) ENGINE HEALTH: no performance credit for above specification power (positive power margin). Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-26.

s92-perf-002.text: Per WIND ACCOUNTABILITY, unless otherwise authorized by operating regulations, what performance credit/penalty applies to headwind and tailwind components? -- Correct: No more than 50% credit for the headwind performance increase, and 150% penalty applied to the tailwind performance decrement. The pilot is not authorized to credit more than 50 percent of the performance increase from an actual headwind, and must reduce performance by 150 percent of the decrement resulting from an actual tailwind component.
s92-perf-002.note: p.4-1 (DOC 213) WIND ACCOUNTABILITY: not more than 50 percent of headwind increase; reduce by 150 percent of tailwind decrement. Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-26.

s92-perf-003.text: For the Category A horizontal takeoff procedure, in what range and increments is the Takeoff Decision Point (TDP) airspeed selectable, and how is Vtoss defined? -- Correct: Selectable in 1-knot increments between 30 and 48 knots; Vtoss = TDP + 15 knots. TDP is selectable in 1-knot increments between 30 and 48 knots, with Vtoss defined as TDP + 15 knots, permitting payload to be traded against available field length.
s92-perf-003.note: p.4-1 (DOC 213): TDP selectable in 1 knot increments between 30 and 48 knots; Vtoss = TDP + 15 knots. Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-26.

s92-perf-004.text: What two operational questions does the S-92 Category A variable-TDP takeoff procedure allow a pilot to answer? -- Correct: Determine the maximum takeoff gross weight for an available field length, or determine the required field length for a desired takeoff gross weight. The variable-TDP Category A procedure lets a pilot trade payload against available field length: given a field length, determine the maximum takeoff gross weight; or given a desired takeoff gross weight, determine the required field length.
s92-perf-004.note: p.4-1 (DOC 213): max takeoff gross weight given field length; required field length given desired weight. Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-26.

s92-perf-005.text: How does a lower TDP speed affect Category A rejected/continued takeoff field length and maximum takeoff gross weight? -- Correct: A lower TDP speed gives shorter RTO/CTO field lengths but also a lower maximum takeoff gross weight. RTO and CTO distances, and maximum takeoff/landing gross weight, are both directly proportional to TDP speed: lower TDP speeds mean shorter field lengths but also lower maximum gross weights, and vice versa.
s92-perf-005.note: p.4-1 (DOC 213): RTO/CTO distances and max takeoff/landing gross weight directly proportional to TDP speed. Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-26.

s92-perf-006.text: For a Category A ground level helipad takeoff, what does the "maximum reject TDP" represent? -- Correct: The highest height from which a rejected landing can be accomplished without damage to the aircraft. The maximum reject TDP is the highest height from which a rejected landing can be accomplished without damage to the aircraft, as distinct from the minimum fly-away TDP.
s92-perf-006.note: p.4-2 (DOC 214): maximum reject TDP is the highest height from which a rejected landing can be accomplished without damage. Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-26.

s92-perf-007.text: For a Category A ground level helipad takeoff, what does the "minimum fly-away TDP" represent? -- Correct: The lowest height from which the fly-away maneuver can be accomplished with 15 feet of clearance from the helipad altitude. The minimum fly-away TDP is the lowest height from which the fly-away maneuver can be accomplished with 15 feet of clearance from the helipad altitude.
s92-perf-007.note: p.4-2 (DOC 214): minimum fly away TDP is the lowest height for the fly away with 15 feet clearance from helipad altitude. Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-26.

s92-perf-008.text: What safety concern arises if the minimum fly-away TDP is greater than the maximum reject TDP for a given weight/altitude/temperature? -- Correct: Safe continued flight or landing is not assured if an engine fails while climbing between the two TDPs. If the minimum fly-away TDP exceeds the maximum reject TDP, safe continued flight or landing is not assured for an engine failure occurring while climbing between the two TDPs.
s92-perf-008.note: p.4-2 (DOC 214) CAUTION: min fly away TDP greater than max reject TDP -> safe continued flight or landing not assured between the two TDPs. Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-26.

s92-perf-009.text: How is the Category A ground level helipad "take off field length" defined? -- Correct: The horizontal distance from the helipad required to reach 35 feet above the helipad or obstacle altitude at a Vtoss climb with 2 minute power selected, after an engine failure at the minimum TDP. Take off field length is the horizontal distance, measured from the helipad, required to reach 35 feet above the helipad or obstacle altitude at a Vtoss climb with 2 minute power selected, following an engine failure at the minimum TDP.
s92-perf-009.note: p.4-2 (DOC 214): take off field length to 35 feet above helipad or obstacle at a Vtoss climb, 2 minute power, engine failure at minimum TDP. Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-26.

s92-perf-010.text: How is the Category A ground level helipad "balked landing distance" defined? -- Correct: The horizontal distance from the helipad required to reach 45 feet above the helipad, or 35 feet above the obstacle (whichever is higher), at a Vtoss climb after an engine failure at the LDP. Balked landing distance is the horizontal distance from the helipad required to reach 45 feet above the helipad or 35 feet above the obstacle, whichever is higher, at a Vtoss climb following an engine failure at the LDP.
s92-perf-010.note: p.4-2 (DOC 214): balked landing distance to 45 feet above the helipad or 35 above the obstacle, whichever higher, Vtoss climb, failure at LDP. Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-26.

s92-perf-011.text: If there are no obstacles over 10 feet in the balked landing path, what minimum Landing Decision Point (LDP) may the pilot choose? -- Correct: 125 feet, providing 25 feet of clearance above helipad level (15 feet clearance of a 10 foot obstacle). With no obstacles over 10 feet in the balked landing path, the pilot can choose the minimum LDP of 125 feet, providing 25 feet of clearance above helipad level (15 feet of clearance over a 10 foot obstacle).

s92-perf-012.text: For a Category A vertical takeoff, if an obstacle is close enough to and low enough over the helipad that it lies within the obstacle exempt region, how must the pilot treat it when determining minimum fly-away TDP? -- Correct: It can be disregarded — no correction to the minimum fly-away TDP is required. Obstacles within the defined obstacle exempt region are guaranteed at least 15 feet of clearance along the takeoff profile due to their low height and close proximity to the pad, and are therefore exempt from obstacle clearance consideration when determining minimum fly-away TDP.
s92-perf-012.note: p.4-37/4-38 (DOC 246-247) Figure 4-19: obstacle in the exempt region may be disregarded, no correction to minimum fly away TDP. Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-26.

s92-perf-013.text: For a Category A vertical takeoff, if an obstacle lies outside the obstacle exempt region (i.e. it is high enough and/or far enough from the pad), what must the pilot do to the minimum fly-away TDP? -- Correct: Correct it by adding the obstacle height to the no-obstacle minimum fly-away TDP. If an obstacle falls outside the obstacle exempt region, the minimum fly-away TDP must be corrected by adding the obstacle height to it; if that corrected TDP then exceeds the maximum reject TDP, a Category A takeoff cannot be performed for the planned weight, altitude, temperature and obstacle.

s92-perf-015.text: What is the fundamental performance guarantee that distinguishes a correctly flown Category A takeoff/landing from a Category B one? -- Correct: Category A, flown within the approved weight/altitude/temperature/field-length/wind conditions, guarantees continued safe flight and landing after an engine failure; Category B does not provide this guarantee. Category A takeoff and landing procedures, flown at the approved weight, altitude, temperature, field length and wind conditions, guarantee continued safe flight and landing after an engine failure. Operating outside those approved conditions, or under Category B, does not carry this guarantee.

s92-perf-016.text: During Category A takeoff and landing maneuvers, what is the Non-Flying Pilot's (NFP) role with respect to TDP/LDP? -- Correct: Announce when the aircraft attains the TDP or LDP airspeed and/or altitude, and call out deviations from required performance parameters. The Non-Flying Pilot supports the Flying Pilot by announcing when the aircraft attains the TDP or LDP airspeed/altitude, and by calling out when actual performance (e.g. Nr range, ground track, or Vtoss) deviates from what is required for the maneuver.
